title: Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Billy Evans Admits ‘She Looks Insane’ in ‘You Can See Everything’ Trailer but Defends Making the Doc: ‘Make Up Your Own Mind’
description: Elizabeth Holmes‘ partner Billy Evans appeared on the “All-In” podcast just as Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary “You Can See Everyt
body:
Elizabeth Holmes‘ partner Billy Evans appeared on the “All-In” podcast just as Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary “You Can See Everything” started its theatrical release to explain why the couple allowed a camera crew inside their home in the days leading up to Holmes going to prison. Evans has not yet seen the movie, which has earned universal acclaim and Oscar buzz since world premiering at the Telluride Film Festival last month.
	

	“[The context going in] is Elizabeth is facing an 11-year sentence. She’s been prevented from speaking publicly in any way, shape or form and this would come out after that period in which she is now allowed to talk,” Evans said. “There’s been a lot of media produced on her. There’s been a lot of people who have told her story. That narrative is pretty ossified. The whole idea was here she is, see her and make up your own mind. It’s not to re-litigate the case. Practically, at this time she was not allowed to talk about the case, so she was gonna follow the rules and not talk about the case.”


	“It was to have people see who she is,” he continued. “I have gone through this consistent experience with the people who love me most, from my grandmother to my best friends. They’d hear I knew [Elizabeth Holmes] or I was falling for this person and now we’re going to have a kid… in the beginning, every single one of these people thought I was crazy. ‘Do you know who she is?’ I would tell them, ‘I understand why you feel that way but just meet her.’ And they would meet her and spend time with her and see her in a totally natural environment, like going on a hike or helping a friend. Every opinion of her would radically shift. That was the intention of the film. To help scale that up and allow other people to sit with her and make up their own minds.”
	

	However, it would appear Holmes and Evans’ decision is backfiring. “You Can See Everything” has only amplified the backlash against and the distrust of former Theranos CEO Holmes. Even before the movie screened for press, A24 dropped a chilling teaser trailer that had many viewers disturbed by Holmes’ demeanor and claims that she did not do anything wrong at Theronos.

	“I haven’t seen it. I might think this is the dumbest thing I have ever done,” Evans said on the podcast, admitting that Holmes “looks insane” in the trailer and acknowledging that “especially the music” in the clip has an anti-Holmes bent.

	“Am I nervous? I have been through so many intense, surreal experiences that it takes a bit to raise my blood pressure,” Evans said. “With this there’s certainly concern but it’s ultimately our decision.”

	Holmes and Evans met in 2017 and had their first child, William, in 2021. Their daughter, Invicta, was born in 2023. Watch Evans’ full interview on the “All-In” podcast in the video below.

schema.headline: Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Billy Evans Admits ‘She Looks Insane’ in ‘You Can See Everything’ Trailer but Defends Making the Doc: ‘Make Up Your Own Mind’

title: Music Industry Moves: My Chemical Romance Signs With Warner Chappell
description: Warner Chappell Music, the music publishing arm of Warner Music Group, has signed an exclusive worldwide administration agreement with veteran New
body:
Warner Chappell Music, the music publishing arm of Warner Music Group, has signed an exclusive worldwide administration agreement with veteran New Jersey rock band My Chemical Romance. The partnership covers the global publishing administration of the band’s entire catalog, including their albums “Three Cheers for Sweet Revenge,” “The Black Parade,” and more, alongside future works.

	Under the new global agreement, WCM will oversee global rights administration, copyright protection, bespoke sync licensing across film, television, and video games, while pursuing creative opportunities. The new publishing agreement expands on My Chemical Romance’s long-term relationship with Warner Records, which began in 2003, and their global merchandise partnership through WMG.
	

	+ Payday Music Publishing has extended its relationship representing Grammy-nominated singer-songwriter Hayla, who has been represented by the company since 2023 and has been featured on songs by John Summit, Illenium and others.


	“Patrick and the whole Payday team have been nothing but fully supportive of Hayla over the last few years,” said Hayla’s manager Jon Vick of Restless Minds Music. “They have created incredible environments to enable Hayla to write and perform on extraordinary songs.”

	+ Belgium-born producer-songwriter Oliver Symons has signed with the Maison Arts label, premiering the partnership with the song “Wake Up” and planning a “prolific” release schedule for the coming months. He originally made his name as the main producer and a member of the Benelux group Bazart before going solo and collaborating with Alessandro Buccellati (Lily Allen, SZA), Gianluca Buccellati (Lana Del Rey, Arlo Parks) and, most recently, Nathan Boddy (James Blake, Olivia Dean, PinkPantheress).
	

	+ Sony Music Publishing Nashville has signed singer-songwriter Payton Sullivan to a worldwide publishing deal.

	“Any team that’ll wear bikini top T-shirts for you is a ride-or-die team!,” he said “I’ve been writing songs since I was five, and dreaming of this life in my bedroom, so joining Rusty, Tom, and everyone at Sony Music Publishing means the world,” shared Sullivan. “None of this would be possible without the songs, and I can’t wait to write the next chapter with them.”

	Wednesday, October 16

	Mohnish Sani has joined Hybe Americas in the newly created role of Head of Strategy and Growth, the company announced on Wednesday. In the role he will focus on long-term growth across the Americas markets and work with Hybe Korea’s strategy team; he will be based in New York and will report to Hybe Americas CEO Isaac Lee.

	Prior to joining Hybe, Sani served as Head of Strategy & Operations for Creator Services at Amazon Entertainment. Before that role, he managed global digital licensing and content acquisition at YouTube Music, along with roles Amazon Music, Kobalt Music Group and Sony Music.

	+ British band Adult Leisure has signed with Big Loud Rock, as the band’s single “Kiss Me Like You Miss Her” impacts on alternative radio.

	”We’re happy to finally say that we’ve signed with Big Loud Rock,” the Bristol-based band said in a statement. “Over the last few months, we’ve had the pleasure of getting to know everyone, talking about what’s next for us, and working out what we are building together. It feels like we’ve found the right people at the right time, and we can’t wait to get started.”

	Big Loud Co-Founder and Big Loud Rock President Joey Moi added, “It’s rare to see a U.K. alt-indie band connect this quickly over here right out of the gate, but the early radio support behind “Kiss Me Like You Miss Her” just tells you everything. We’re excited to officially welcome Adult Leisure to the Big Loud Rock family, and can’t wait to keep this momentum going stateside.”

	+ Revolution Music Group has named Allen Wollard president of its newly formed recorded music division. In this role, he will oversee all aspects of the record label’s operations, including artist and repertoire, marketing, and business strategy. Previously, Wollard held leadership roles at Sunshine Entertainment, the Wright Group, Silver Wave Records and Garden City Music.
	

	“Mr. Wollard is exactly the type of leader we need at this time for Revolution Records,” said COO Raymond Davis RMG. “He has a rare combination of creative instinct and business acumen, along with a track record of building projects that don’t just perform — they last.”

	Tuesday, Oct. 13

	Singer-songwriter-actress and Chrome Hearts co-creative director Jesse Jo Stark has signed with WME for worldwide representation in all areas.

	Stark’s new album “Muse” is out Nov. 6, which follows dates opening for or performing with Post Malone, Guns N’ Roses and Jane’s Addiction, as well as multiple festival appearances. In addition to her work at Chrome Hearts, Stark also helms the clothing line Deadly Doll.

	+ Veteran music executive Rebecca Allen is leaving Universal Music Group U.K. after 27 years, according to Music Week. She will continue in an advisory role at UMG.

	Following the merger of EMI and Island in July 2024, Allen was appointed as president of the new Audience & Media division, and subsequently promoted to the newly-formed, “first-of-its-kind” leadership role of chief artist and strategy officer in December 2025. Previously, she was president and later co-president of the relaunched EMI (alongside Jo Charrington), following her role as president of Decca from 2017 to 2020 – becoming the first female president at a Universal Music U.K. label.

	“I leave enormously proud of what we’ve created together, grateful for the friendships, the adventures, the lessons and the laughter, and for 27 years that have shaped me in more ways than I probably even realise yet,” Allen wrote in a farewell letter to staff, per MW. “It’s been quite a ride. I can’t thank you all enough for being on this journey with me. Love to you all.”

	+ Sony Music Publishing Colombia has entered into a global catalog administration agreement with the Estate of acclaimed Colombian singer, songwriter and accordionist Omar Geles, one of the most influential artists to work in vallenato music. The agreement encompasses more than three-hundred celebrated works penned by the Latin-Grammy nominated songwriter including the vallenato anthem “Cuatro Rosas,” as well as classics such as “A Blanco y Negro,” “Tu Hombre Soy Yo” and “Tarde lo Conocí.”
	

	“In the name of my family and the Omar Geles state, we want to extend our most sincere gratitude for opening your doors and allow us to be part of the Sony Music Publishing family,” said Maren García. “We hope to build a relationship based in trust, respect, and the commitment of continuing to take Omar Geles’ legacy to new generations. Thanks for making us feel at home since the first moment and for continuing to write the history of the legacy of my eternal love, a legacy that will continue to live in each one of his songs.”

	Jorge Mejía, President and CEO, Latin America and U.S. Latin, Sony Music Publishing said, “Omar Geles was not only a defining voice in vallenato music, but one of the great songwriters of his generation. It is a true honor to partner with his family to preserve, promote and expand his legacy, ensuring that his songs continue to inspire audiences around the world for generations to come.”

	+ The Music Publishers Association, the U.K. trade body representing music publishers, has named Faber Music CEO Richard King as its new Board Chair for a three-year term, following a vote by its Board of Directors. He succeeds Paulette Long OBE, who remains an MPA Board Director following the conclusion of her term as Chair.

	Having served as CEO of leading independent music publisher Faber Music since 1999, King brings more than 25 years of publishing leadership to the role, with experience spanning classical, film and TV, pop and printed music. He previously served as an MPA Director from 2002 to 2019 before rejoining the Board in 2022. He was a PRS director for 18 years to 2022, a Director of PRS Foundation for 9 years to 2024 and has been a Director of PML since its inception in 2012. King will work alongside Peter Jackson, who joined the MPA as Managing Director in July.

	“I’m looking forward to building on the great work of Paulette and the MPA executive team, particularly by using my experience as a music publisher to further amplify our sector’s voice on the issues that matter most to members,” King said. “There is plenty to build on. The Government’s recently announced Plan for Music and new National Plan for Music Education are welcome steps, but we need to ensure these initiatives lead to meaningful, sustained long-term change. At a time of enormous change, it is more important than ever that music publishers have a strong and unified voice.”
	

	Paul Clements, CEO of the MPA Group, added, “Richard has been an important voice within the MPA for many years and I know he will bring fresh thinking, challenge and real ambition to the role of Chair. Peter has already made a huge impact since joining us, bringing new energy and ideas to the team and a clear vision for how we can do even more for our members.

	“I’d also like to thank Paulette for her outstanding leadership and contribution as Chair. With Richard leading the Board and Peter driving the MPA forward day-to-day, we have a brilliant team in place for this next chapter.”

title: Timothy Busfield Indictment on Child Sex Abuse Charges Thrown Out by Judge
description: A New Mexico judge on Friday threw out an indictment against actor Timothy Busfield, finding that prosecutors failed to act in an impartial manner
body:
A New Mexico judge on Friday threw out an indictment against actor Timothy Busfield, finding that prosecutors failed to act in an impartial manner during the grand jury proceedings.

	Busfield was indicted in February on charges of groping a 7-year-old boy on the set of “The Cleaning Lady,” a Fox show on which he worked as a director. He maintains his innocence.

	In his ruling, Judge Joseph Montano found that prosecutors had impeded grand jurors who wanted to hear from defense witnesses. Some eight potential witnesses were sitting in the hallway outside, but were not called to appear.
	

	“The prosecuting attorney failed to act in a fair and impartial manner, including the failure to properly instruct the grand jury on the law for calling witnesses and in instructing the grand jurors on a procedure that effectively withheld requested witnesses,” the judge wrote. “In doing so, the grand jury proceedings were conducted in a manner that violated grand jury statutes designed to protect the structural integrity of our grand jury system and the presumption of prejudice applies.”

	Prosecutors have the option of seeking another indictment, but have yet to decide whether to do that.

	“Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed,” said a spokesperson for the Second Judicial District Attorney in Albuquerque.

	Busfield, best known as a star of “The West Wing” and “Thirtysomething,” was accused of groping a boy who worked as a child actor on “The Cleaning Lady” in 2022. In an interview with investigators, Busfield said that the boys’ parents were seeking “revenge” after the boys were not hired for the show’s final season.
	

	Busfield’s attorneys had him take a polygraph test, which he passed. Warner Bros. TV, which produced the show, conducted its own investigation after a separate allegation was raised through SAG-AFTRA in late 2024. The WBTV investigation was unable to substantiate the claim.

	Busfield and an Albuquerque police detective were the only two witnesses to appear before the grand jury. During his testimony, Busfield cited the WBTV investigation and said that other witnesses would be able to testify.

	According to the ruling, some of the grand jurors asked to hear from additional witnesses on three occasions. However, the prosecutor told them that at least eight of them would have to agree in order for a subpoena to be issued, and that all 12 would have to return on a later date to hear that testimony.

	The judge stated that no such requirements exist, noting that the witnesses were in the hall. The judge found that this had “the practical effect of unilaterally withholding witnesses requested by the grand jurors.” 

	“These actions are not in line with either the letter or the spirit of the grand jury laws,” Montano concluded.

	Amber Fayerberg, Busfield’s attorney, said that he is “relieved and grateful today.”

	“The grand jurors kept asking to hear from the people who were on set with him,” she said. “Those witnesses were sitting in the hallway, ready to tell the grand jury what they saw, and what they saw shows that Tim is innocent. The prosecution would not let them in, and the Court saw that for what it was: a violation of the grand jury laws that protect the integrity of our justice system. We know this may not be the end. If the State chooses to try again, Tim is ready, and so are those witnesses.”

schema.headline: Timothy Busfield Indictment on Child Sex Abuse Charges Thrown Out by Judge

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Surprise Screens at London Film Festival
description: London Film Festival‘s surprise film on Friday night was “I Play Rocky,” Peter Farrelly’s biographical drama about the beginnings of Sylvester Stal
body:
London Film Festival‘s surprise film on Friday night was “I Play Rocky,” Peter Farrelly’s biographical drama about the beginnings of Sylvester Stallone‘s beloved boxing franchise.

	Farrelly was on hand to introduce the movie and shouted out his star, newcomer Anthony Ippolito, who has already earned praise for his portrayal of Stallone. “I could do a TED talk about Anthony Ippolito. This kid is ridiculous,” Farrelly said, adding that the 27-year-old sent in a self-tape before the film team even began what was meant to be a “worldwide search” for who would play Stallone.
	

	“He heard about the movie, tracked down the script, shot three scenes in his grandmother’s basement on Long Island and sent it to us,” Farrelly continued. “I looked at it like, ‘That’s it.’ We never looked past him.”


	“I Play Rocky” tells the true story of how Stallone, then a young small-time actor, overcame obstacles to both write and star in the 1976 classic. Alongside Ippolito, it stars AnnSophia Robb as Sasha Czack, Stallone’s wife; Matt Dillon as his father, Frank Stallone Sr.; P.J. Byrne as “Rocky” producer Irwin Winkler; Jay Duplass as director John G. Avildsen and more.

	Farrelly added that he’s most proud of the fact that Stallone himself is pleased with the movie. “No matter how well the movie does, how many people like it, if Stallone said, ‘I don’t like it,’ I would be really disappointed,” he said. “And he loved it.”

	The film first premiered at Toronto Film Festival last month, where it was up for the People’s Choice Award and generated positive reviews. Variety‘s chief film critic Owen Gleiberman called the film a “cleverly-crafted crowd pleaser” and praised Ippolito for getting his portrayal of Stallone “just right,” writing: “Watching and listening to Anthony Ippolito, we can believe that Sylvester Stallone is standing right in front of us, though the performance is more than just an awesome impersonation. He’s truly playing Stallone — the sweetly stubborn and dogged person he was at the time.”
	

	“I Play Rocky” is set to hit U.S. and U.K. theaters on Nov. 6.

schema.headline: ‘I Play Rocky’ Surprise Screens at London Film Festival

title: ‘Red Rising’ Movie in the Works at Paramount With ‘Hunger Games’ Director Francis Lawrence
description: Hail Reaper! The rights to the popular “Red Rising” book series have been picked up at Paramount with “Hunger Games” director Francis Lawrence atta
body:
Hail Reaper! The rights to the popular “Red Rising” book series have been picked up at Paramount with “Hunger Games” director Francis Lawrence attached to a movie based on the first novel.

	Justin Rhodes will write the script, based on the original 2014 novel by author Pierce Brown. Lawrence and Cameron MacConomy will produce for About.Blank, alongside Francesco Goedhuis. Brown will executive produce.


	“Red Rising” takes place in a sci-fi future where planets have been colonized and society has been separated into a color-coded caste system. The impoverished Reds work as slave labor in the mines of Mars, while the super-strong Golds rule the solar system and war on each other. The books follow Darrow of Lykos, a miner who suffers a great loss and is thrust into a rebellion’s revenge plot against the Golds. He undergoes a brutal transformation to become a Gold himself and enrolls at a military school alongside other young adults who are tested before joining the highest Gold ranks. There are currently six books in the series, including “Golden Son,” “Morning Star,” “Iron Gold,” “Dark Age” and “Lightbringer,” with a seventh and final novel, “Red God,” on the way.
	

	Lawrence is no stranger to adapting popular young adult novels. He’s directed every “Hunger Games” movie, including next month’s prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping” and 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.” He also directed last year’s Stephen King adaptation “The Long Walk.”

	Lawrence is repped by CAA, Gretchen Rush at Hansen Jacobson and ID. Brown is repped by CAA, Hannah Bowman at Liza Dawson Associates for publishin  and Dave Feldman at Brecheen Feldman Breimer Silver & Thompson. Rhodes is repped by CAA, Adam Kolbrenner at Lit Entertainment and Eric Suddleson at Toczek Suddleson.
	

	The Hollywood Reporter first broke the news.

schema.headline: ‘Red Rising’ Movie in the Works at Paramount With ‘Hunger Games’ Director Francis Lawrence

title: The Best Horror Movies of 2026 (So Far), Ranked: ‘Obsession,’ ‘Resident Evil,’ ‘Backrooms’ and More
description:
Oct 16, 2026 1:23pm PT	
	

	
		The Best Horror Movies of 2026 (So Far), Ranked: ‘Obsession,’ ‘Resident Evil,’ ‘Backrooms’ and More
body:
Oct 16, 2026 1:23pm PT	
	

	
		The Best Horror Movies of 2026 (So Far), Ranked: ‘Obsession,’ ‘Resident Evil,’ ‘Backrooms’ and More
	
	
			


			
			
	

									©Mubi/Courtesy Everett Collection / Courtesy Everett Collection / ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection / ©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection
	

		
	
				

	2026 has already been a wild year for horror, from low-budget box office hits (“Backrooms,” “Obsession”) to sequels the world could have lived without (“Scream 7,” “The Strangers – Chapter 3”). In a year loaded with scary movies, many of them were good-to-great, a welcome surprise that kept multiplexes busy. Below are the year’s standouts, including some honorable mentions also worth watching. 

	There were also several exciting genre movies released this year — such as Adam Wingard’s “Onslaught,” Na Hong-jin’s “Hope” and David Robert Mitchell’s “The End of Oak Street” — that flirted with being horror, but ultimately seemed to fit better in categories like action, sci-fi and adventure.

	Note: Only films that were fully released in 2026 so far were up for inclusion, so no festival favorites or titles that haven’t hit theaters yet — like Zachary Wigon’s “Victorian Psycho” or Robert Eggers’ “Werwulf”— could make the cut.

	Honorable Mentions: 

	Send Help (20th Century Studios) — Sam Raimi’s return to horror was this stylish little survival thriller, with great performances from Rachel McAdams and Dylan O’Brien as two at-odds office workers who are trying to get off a deserted island after a gnarly plane crash. While the overarching plot is a little predictable, there are some great twists and turns along the way. 

	Buffet Infinity (Yellow Veil Pictures) — This wild feature made up entirely of fake commercials is a trip to watch, and will delight any fans “Tim and Eric Awesome Show, Great Job!” or other lost media madness. Although the clips feel disconnected at first, it’s soon clear that a local sinkhole might be behind a restaurant war, a religious cult and plenty more unpredictable twists and turns. It’s not for everybody, but those who can get on the same wavelength as “Buffet Infinity” will be richly rewarded. 

	Saccharine (Independent Film Company and Shudder) — Natalie Erika James’ timely film considers the dark side of fad diets, as a med student (Midori Francis) realizes that ingesting the ashes of the dead is the best miracle drug around. While it’s not the white-knuckle ride many fans might want, it’s an effectively gross body horror story that has plenty to say.


			
			
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	A24

	Kane Parsons’ dizzyingly accomplished film is a masterwork in tone and tension, dropping Chiwetel Ejiofor and Renate Reinsve into an endless maze of liminal spaces that are claustrophobic, confusing and overwhelming. It’s hard to describe why “Backrooms” works to the unconverted or unconvinced, but the incredible production design and camerawork of Jeremy Cox make up for any limitations of the sketch of a script. It’s exciting to see what Parsons will do with a next chapter — and maybe even what he could do beyond the limitations of his own space.

		
			
			
	Exit 8
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Toho, Cannes Film Festival
				
					
				

	Neon

	Genki Kawamura’s video game adaptation concerns a man (Kazunari Ninomiya) who cannot escape walking a long section of a subway hallway, stuck in an endless repetition. Yet he’s soon able to discern tiny clues about how to move forward and pass through some dark reverberations of his life and decisions to get to the other side. While the hook grows a little thin, it’s by necessity, as the audience begins to feel as stuck and hopeless as its main character, and each new detail pointing to escape is a breath of fresh air.

		
			
			
	Mārama
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Dark Sky Films and Watermelon Pictures

	Taratoa Stappard’s gothic tale examines Māori culture and the colonizers who almost snuffed it out. Ariāna Osborne is spellbinding as the title character, a Victorian-era woman who travels to England to find out more about her lineage, only to become a governess for a mysterious man with an affinity for her Māori heritage. As things get dark, Stappard’s vision grows even more lush, with an atmosphere teeming with evil.

		
			
			
	Faces of Death
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Independent Film Company and Shudder				
					
				

	Independent Film Company

	The idea of releasing a new “Faces of Death” may have once seemed inconceivable, but the creative partnership of Isa Mazzei and Daniel Goldhaber was able to spin the seminal oddity into a tight serial killer movie with a deeper motive. Dacre Montgomery plays a maniac obsessed with the original film, which was purported to include real-life depictions of violence. His recreation of the goriest bits nabs the attention of a content moderator (Barbie Ferreira) and a bloody game of cat and mouse begins. Mazzei and Goldhaber have plenty of keen observations on influencer and online culture, while Montgomery is genuinely chilling as a killer who does his best to blend in and be forgettable.

		
			
			
	28 Years Later: The Bone Temple
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Sony Pictures Releasing

	A heady, heartfelt spin on zombie movies, Nia DaCosta helms this fourth chapter in the series, which dodges nearly every expectation. Ralph Fiennes stars as Dr. Ian Kelson, who lives alone in the post-breakout world, coming closer and closer to finding a cure with the help of his undead friend, Samson (Chi Lewis-Parry). Unfortunately, as the pair develops a partnership, a roving leader of violent kids, Sir Lord Jimmy Crystal (Jack O’Connell), roams the countryside looking for people to antagonize. Many thought-provoking moments — as well as one wild Iron Maiden dance sequence — follow in Alex Garland’s sharp script, which begs for another installment.

		
			
			
	Leviticus
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Neon				
					
				

	Neon

	A touching love story about two boys in Australia becomes a nightmare when a religious conversion therapy turns the person they love the most into the thing trying to kill them. From there, Naim (Joe Bird) and Ryan (Stacy Clausen) are unsure if the object of their affection is real or a beast out for blood. Building a heartfelt and tender romance, “Leviticus” traffics more in tension than flat-out scares, but it’s unlikely there will be a more affecting horror movie this year.

		
			
			
	They Will Kill You
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures				
					
				

	Warner Bros. Pictures

	Zazie Beetz kicks an enormous amount of ass as brutal fighter Asia Reaves in this horror-action-comedy. When she infiltrates a hotel that she believes has kidnapped her maid sister, Asia must brawl her way through endless villains loyal to the satanic cult, who are invincible but can get mutilated along the way, leading to surreal scenes like the adventures of a dislodged, crawling eyeball. An early “Kill Bill”-esque showdown and a torch-lit beatdown in a ballroom are among the flashy setpieces. Beetz is a pro at the stunt choreography, showing the toil of inflicting and receiving extreme pain. Cinematographer Isaac Bauman also shoots her in inspired ways, touching on pop touchstones like comic books and martial arts films.

		
			
			
	Appofeniacs
			
										
					Image Credit: Magenta Edge Films				
					
				

	Magenta Edge Films

	An internet troll with an axe to grind sets off this interwoven tale of mayhem from first-time feature director Chris Marrs Piliero. This microbudget thriller stretches out every dollar for a visually inventive look at how deepfakes can disrupt the lives of people even after they log off. Filled with shocking twists and some great practical effects, it’s a film as funny and squirm-inducing as it is prescient.

		
			
			
	Her Private Hell
			
										
					Image Credit: Neon				
					
				

	Neon

	Nicolas Winding Refn’s received a flurry of mixed-to-negative reviews, but ignore them. No one is making films like Refn, and if you can get on his wavelength, it’s a hell of a ride worth taking. Sophie Thatcher, Charles Melton and Havana Rose Liu are hypnotic in this giallo-influenced head trip. Endlessly stylish and bold, “Her Private Hell” is destined for cult classic status.

		
			
			
	Resident Evil
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Sony Pictures Releasing

	Third time’s a charm, as Zach Cregger cements his winning run as a horror auteur with this roller coaster ride of a video game adaptation. Austin Abrams is a perfect audience surrogate, injecting humor into the increasingly outrageous situations as his life quickly becomes a zombie-fueled chase. It’s a completely different vibe from both “Barbarian” and “Weapons,” and it’s so exciting to think about what Cregger has up his sleeve next.

		
			
			
	Touch Me
			
										
					Image Credit: Dustin Supencheck				
					
				

	Yellow Veil Pictures

	Addison Heimann’s wild take on an alien creature feature blends up countless inspirations: tentacle sex, drugs, Japanese cinema, ‘80s hip-hop dance and throuples, to name a few. Yet it’s a kaleidoscopic adventure: A slacker (Olivia Taylor Dudley) and her gay best friend (Jordan Gavaris) both start hooking up with an extraterrestrial (Lou Taylor Pucci) whose powers make them feel like they’re in a drug-fueled euphoria. Unfortunately, the alien has a darker plan than he lets on, and our unlikely heroes must save humanity. With plenty of humor and unpredictable moments, it’s a joy to take a ride in Heimann’s mind.

		
			
			
	Hokum
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Neon				
					
				

	Neon

	An old-school haunted house bonanza, Damian McCarthy’s latest drops Ohm (Adam Scott) into an Irish hotel that’s filled with secrets. When he gets locked in, he has to solve a murder mystery before he’s overtaken by scores of supernatural happenings. The set design is remarkable, toeing the line between coziness and mustiness that makes the hotel come alive for all of the senses. Scott is a remarkable lead, as he’s playing Ohm as such an asshole, but his journey of self-awareness soon becomes as engaging as what happened to the dead body. It’s all threaded by some highbrow jump scares that make for a great rollercoaster ride, best enjoyed at a crowded multiplex.

		
			
			
	Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of MUBI				
					
				

	Mubi

	Jane Schoenbrun’s winning rom-com is rooted in an obsessive love for slashers, and begs for repeat viewings to luxuriate in all of the pop culture nods embedded within. But the film is not merely a pastiche: Hannah Einbinder and Gillian Anderson have crackling chemistry together, and the film is filled with indelible imagery and memorable scenes, from a sexually charged KFC dinner to a spirited massacre scene soundtracked to Counting Crows.

		
			
			
	Obsession
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Focus Features/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Focus Features

	Before all of the thinkpieces and analysis, “Obsession” started life as a nasty little thriller that mixed an old-school monkey’s paw scenario with a contemporary look at life in the friendzone. It’s a simple story, but twisty scares and an all-timer performance from Inde Navarrette made the fear burrow deep into audiences’ minds. Countless WTF moments have been debated for months, and that bleak ending ensured the film stayed unforgettable long after leaving the theater.

		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

title: ‘True Detective’ Season 5: Antonio Banderas Joins Nicolas Cage as Series Set to Film in 2027

body:
Antonio Banderas has joined Nicolas Cage in “True Detective” Season 5.

	The duo will headline the next installment of the HBO anthology series, which is set to begin production in 2027.

	The new season hails from showrunner Issa López, who helmed the Alaska-set fourth season, “Night Country,” starring Jodie Foster and Kali Reis. Season 5 will take place in Jamaica Bay, New York.


	Few character details are known, but Banderas will star as Rai García while Cage will play the role of Henry Logan. 
	

	López is the writer and director, executive producing alongside writer Daniel Zelman as well as Mari Jo Winkler, Kathleen McCaffrey, Cage, Banderas, Steve Golin, Richard Brown, Nic Pizzolatto, Cary Joji Fukunaga, Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey.

	Created by Pizzolatto, “True Detective” has been nominated for 41 Emmys and has won six, including for actors Harrelson, McConaughey, Ali and Foster. Per HBO, Season 4 was the most-watched installment of the show to date, with 12.7 million cross-platform viewers.

	Banderas is coming off of celebrated roles in the Anthony Bourdain biopic “Tony” as well as the Nicole Kidman-led “Babygirl.” He also starred in “The Mask of Zorro” and “The Legend of Zorro” and voices Puss in Boots in the Shrek franchise.

	Cage is best known for “Pig,” “Dream Scenario,” “Leaving Las Vegas” and, of course, “National Treasure.” “True Detective” marks just the second lead television role in his career, following his performance in the dark superhero series “Spider-Noir.”

	Banderas is represented by NuCo Media Group and Greenberg Glusker. Cage is represented by WME, Stride Management and attorney Patrick Knapp.

title: Selma Blair’s Rep Speaks Out After Actress’ Arrest and Plane Incident: ‘Selma Did Not Intend to Harm Anyone’
description: Selma Blair‘s spokesperson has spoken out after the actress was charged with second-degree assault following a violent incident on a Delta flight o
body:
Selma Blair‘s spokesperson has spoken out after the actress was charged with second-degree assault following a violent incident on a Delta flight on Sunday.

	“Since Sunday night, the public account of what happened to Selma aboard a flight to New York has been built almost entirely on a police statement and a decade-old headline,” her spokesperson told People.

	“A handful of journalists have taken the time to report on Selma as a human being rather than a headline, and we are grateful to them,” the statement continued. “But fair reporting has been the exception, and in the space left by our silence, speculation has hardened into something being treated as fact. We can, however, correct the record on a few points already in public circulation. Selma Blair experienced a medical emergency on the flight. There was no attempt to open the door of the aircraft. Selma did not intend to harm anyone.”
	

	The spokesperson added, “The suggestion by anyone that Selma does not have multiple sclerosis is outrageous. Her diagnosis has been public since 2018. What Selma has been able to do physically in the years since is nothing short of a miracle. She still has bad days, and she lives with pain daily. Selma also has pseudobulbar affect, a neurological condition secondary to her MS, which bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her. For the same reason, she travels with a service dog who doesn’t leave her side, and the authorities took her dog from her.”

	Blair “has worked on seven film and television projects in 2026 alone, only a couple of which have been announced. She has launched a skin care line, a clothing line, and a line of eye-glass readers, each built around the idea of beauty and utility for people whose bodies do not always cooperate. She remains a visible and relentless advocate for disability rights, for the MS community, and this year for the Jewish community in the face of rising antisemitism, including from the stage of the ADL’s State of the Arts event at The Jewish Museum two weeks ago. Selma had never been arrested before Sunday night. There is much more to this story than has been reported, and we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion,” the statement concluded.
	

	Blair was arrested on Sunday, Oct. 11 for an incident that occurred after she allegedly punched one flight attendant and bit another on a Delta plane heading from Los Angeles to New York. Law enforcement was waiting for the 54-year-old “Legally Blonde” actress at John F. Kennedy airport, where police took her into custody and transported her to a hospital for evaluation. The arrest was due to her allegedly attacking a police officer and a nurse after being removed from the plane. She could also face federal charges for the incident on board the aircraft. 

	A representative for Blair told Variety: “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is currently in stable condition.”

	The FBI opened an investigation relating to the incident, as the agency does with all assaults aboard aircraft. A Delta Air Lines spokesperson told Variety, “Delta has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first.” Despite the chaos on board, there was no operational impact to the flight, which landed at JFK ahead of schedule at approximately 11 p.m.

	On Monday, Variety reported that Blair had received second-degree assault charges after her arrest, according to Queens Criminal Court. The actress posted $20,000 in bail, paid by credit card, and was released later that evening.

	This incident was not the first time Blair had an outburst on a plane. In 2016, she was removed from a flight on a stretcher while traveling with her 4-year-old son after she “had a total psychotic blackout.” Blair chalked up the incident to drinking a glass of wine and taking a pill, saying at the time, “It was horrible and frightening and I had empathy for myself actually afterwards because it was actually so out of character for me, especially because I’m a mother.”

schema.headline: Selma Blair’s Rep Speaks Out After Actress’ Arrest and Plane Incident: ‘Selma Did Not Intend to Harm Anyone’

title: Kate Berlant on Her HBO Special ‘Parmesan,’ the Joke That Made a Man Flip Her Off and Her Next Project With John Early
description:
There’s a throughline in Kate Berlant’s new HBO special “Parmesan,” and it’s not cheese.

body:
There’s a throughline in Kate Berlant’s new HBO special “Parmesan,” and it’s not cheese.

	“My addiction? My phone,” the comedian says at the beginning of the hour. 

	With slapstick style and performative haughtiness, Berlant yearns for a time before cellphones in the special, out Oct. 16. Chronicling the hyper-niche behaviors that define our online existence, Berlant describes the seemingly inescapable embarrassment of wasting one’s life away in an endless scroll. She delivers verdicts on the great issues of our time, like whether to cover a baby’s face with an emoji or comment “PARMESAN” to receive a link to a pasta recipe. In one of the funniest bits, she talks about watching videos of “unspeakable violence” to “unwind,” like “gorillas fistfighting zookeepers, tourists being eaten by sharks.”
	

	“It makes me long for the past, when maybe you’d numb yourself at the local watering hole,” Berlant tells Variety. “That suddenly feels so quaint. You’d be with your community, and some people would be abusing alcohol in terrifying ways, but at least you’d be together, and you’d be forced to interact with other people.”


	She’s in an Airbnb in San Diego, ripping the “Home Sweet Home” pillows off the bed and couch because “they have hepatitis.”

	“There is this loneliness, which is palpable, and I do think it will drive people into community,” Berlant continues, “because we’ll realize that that’s what we need.”

	
		The first two words of your special are “world’s ending.”	

	Yeah.


	
		Would you describe yourself as a pessimist?	

	You know what’s funny? When I was going to shoot the special, I was like, “I’m not gonna talk about the world ending.” Do I really want to dwell in that fear that we’re all so drenched in? I am not a pessimist, I would say, but I think fear is the appropriate response to the times in which we live, so I would say I have fear.


	
		Fear of what?	

	Generally, I have hope and optimism, and I think there’s a lot of beauty in the world. But I think that we live in a kind of undeniably existentially terrifying moment, and so it felt like it would be insincere or bizarre to not address that ultimately, because I think it is the water that we’re swimming in right now. It’s a strange time, and that also has pulled me toward how lucky I feel to be doing live performance. To me, the beauty of standup is that it is an encounter with actual people, and we are seeing the death of the living arts across all areas of life right now. So I don’t think the special is dark, but I think it acknowledges some of the themes that dominate contemporary life.


	
		I don’t think people will be watching AI comedians.	

	I agree. It will never die. People are always going to want people. I was on a six-week social media cleanse, so I was off for the latest [round of AI paranoia]. I logged back on because my special was announced, and I wanted the dopamine hit. When I was on social media, I saw all the AI stuff, and it really pulled my feet under. And then I deleted it again last night, because I just can’t do it.




	

									EMILIO MADRID
	


	
		You said you just went on a social media cleanse. To what extent is your phone an obstacle to creativity? How do we defeat the endless scroll?	

	We are in the fight for our lives. As far as it being an obstacle to creativity — well it’s complicated. There’s part of me that’s like, “I want to understand the culture.” I love the youth. I don’t want to lose track of where they are, of what they’re looking at. I think that’s really essential. I haven’t figured out how to have an ambient relationship, where you kind of understand, but it’s not completely overtaking your consciousness.

	It’s an obstacle for all of us, whether or not you consider yourself a creative person. It prevents your relationship with yourself and with others. Certainly I procrastinate. My focus has been ravaged by this thing, so I have to reorient myself, and it takes a lot of discipline. I was in school for many years, and I always loved school, and I don’t think I could be in school now.

	
		You joke about having chronic back pain from being an “emerging talent.” Are there other descriptors that have been thrown at you that you’ve grown to resent?	

	Oh my God. I understand why people have said this, but I’ve certainly been branded a “weird comedian” or an “alt comedian,” “left of center.” Sometimes that confuses me, because I have always considered myself quite broad. I cross my goddamn eyes. I identify almost primarily as a physical comedian, and so my act, I hope, is broad. I hope I can reach all different kinds of people.


	
		How do you feel about “character actress”?	

	I think it should be an Oscar category! “Character actress” I embrace with everything I have. I was always going to be a character actress because I have curly hair and I cross my eyes. You’re either an ingénue or a character actress.


	
		You do a bit about incest material being too edgy for the audience. Have you ever told a joke that you felt actually did break a taboo?	

	No. I’ve never been drawn to being perceived as edgy, or in doing edgy material. I don’t think I’ve ever thought, “I went too far.”


	
		I find it interesting that when you ask comedians about their edgiest material, it’s often not what you’d predict. Sometimes it’s not racial or sexual material but, like, some random thing you didn’t realize was touchy.	

	This is really interesting to me: There is a piece of material in this hour that did anger someone, and I was shocked. There’s a joke I have about fathers being like a family friend. I was doing that joke, and I noticed two people get up and leave — center audience. I saw it, but I just thought, “Certainly it’s not about what I’m doing.” And then later I was told it was a man and his wife or partner. And he flipped me off when I said, “A father is a family friend.” And then in the lobby, he threw a glass of wine. I touched a nerve, and I was amazed by that.


	
		That’s wild. Do you know why?	

	Probably he’s feeling a lot of shame or guilt around his parenting.


	
		You talk about your sexuality a lot in the special, saying you’ve “succumbed to a homosexual lifestyle” in recent years. Is it harder to write material when it’s personal?	

	My comedy has always obliquely referenced myself; I’ve never spoken autobiographically about myself. The [off-Broadway] show I did before this, “Kate,” was a send-up of that. So this was my first time ever doing autobiographical material, or actually trying to work through questions about myself that I actually had. Was it harder? No, it just was the only thing I could do. I had done “Kate,” and that consumed my life for a couple of years. And then I was like, “I guess I’m going to try to write stand-up again.” I thought, “So much has changed in my life and in the world. I can’t just pick up where I left off and do that again. I can’t just free-associate and present these caricatures of a person without addressing what was actually going on for me.”

	So it wasn’t harder or easier. It was just the logical next step, because I had just spent two years doing something that was specifically not about myself. Well, it’s all about yourself, always, of course, but I just mean — I created a person who isn’t me. I have an Irish, abusive mother in that show, and that’s not true. So now I was like, “OK, I think I actually have to talk about myself.”


	
		Talk to me about the anti-closer. You hilariously refuse to deliver one final punchline, instead remaining on stage while the audience leaves the room.	

	I chronically struggle to get off stage with stand-up. There’s this pressure of doing a big closer, everyone goes ballistic, and you leave. There’s something inherently embarrassing about it, because you’re reducing yourself to this expectation of the form. It makes sense that you would want to go out on a huge laugh, or that you would tie things up and then leave. That’s logical. But something about it has always … I can’t do it.

	I was doing shows in New York, and one of my oldest friends, Doron Hagay, who directed the special, said, “You need a big closer.” I was thinking about that, and I was like, “It would be funny if I never left.”

	
		You say something like, “I’m gonna watch you for once,” and it reminded me of “Kate,” when you would linger in the lobby before the show with a sign that said “Ignore me.”	

	I know. It’s so funny because I forgot. You can just never get away from yourself. The same questions and ideas and motifs haunt you for the rest of your life. I hadn’t even considered that for my last show I was in the lobby as everyone came in, and now I’m on stage while everyone leaves.

	
		Clearly there’s something about the relationship between audience and performer that interests you.	

	Yeah, what is that? Performance is so strange. It’s such a strange encounter. You come on stage, everyone’s like “yay,” and then you leave. It’s so satisfying. I love it so much. It’s funny how everyone knows their role, which I think is really comforting about seeing something live. For me, the most interesting thing is disrupting that expectation. I’d be remiss if I didn’t admit that I went to a master’s program called Performance Studies, where questions about relationships between audience and performer are investigated.




	

									EMILIO MADRID
	


	
		What is your relationship to fame?	

	I can’t wait to experience being famous.
	

	
		Oh, stop!	

	As an emerging talent, I feel — listen, I am a ham, and always will be one, and so I love any opportunity to be a goof or put on a little show. If somebody comes up to me and likes my comedy, that only makes me excited. I’m not Mariah Carey. My life has not been interrupted by people enjoying my comedy. It’s been enriched by that. But having a persona, being aware of one’s persona — this has all been so chronically amplified by social media. I feel no issue being out in the world, flesh and blood. That’s fine. That’s not complicated for me at all, because I’m not Mariah Carey. Where it’s complicated is navigating that persona and being watched and performing online. That’s this new thing. It’s not so new, but it’s pretty new. That’s what can confuse me or shut me down: how to continue that performance on the internet.


	
		When you were workshopping the act and doing the anti-closer, was it ever difficult logistically? I would imagine that some people wouldn’t want to leave the room because they just want to watch you on stage.	

	People are remarkably respectful and understand it. People are smart. People know what to do. When you say that you’re a stand-up comedian, often one of the first questions you’ll get is, “Oh, do you get heckled?” And that essentially doesn’t exist. That’s a new, perverse obsession of stand-up clips, but that’s not real. It doesn’t really happen. Sure, it has happened in the history of comedy, and I’ve had it a couple of times. I actually had somebody kind of heckling my taping. There was a woman in the front row talking to me, and I had to be like, “Please stop talking to me!” That was hysterical, because it never happens except for that night.


	
		I think the heckling thing has almost been encouraged by the comedians who are putting out the clips. I went to the Comedy Cellar recently and was like, “This is not a participatory art form!”	

	And people are engaging.


	
		Yes. I suppose at many clubs, they have a warm-up act that does almost exclusively crowd work every night.	

	And crowd work is such an art form. I want to be clear: Todd Barry, Moshe Kasher, they’re comedians that do that so beautifully. That’s a different category. That really does exist. But what you’re talking about is a direct symptom of social media and of those clips, and people thinking that’s what going to see comedy is. But even if I perform at a club, most people aren’t doing that to me.

	
		You and John Early have a very beloved creative relationship. This year you starred in his film “Maddie’s Secret.” What are you two working on next?	

	Let’s just say we are ready to have a television show, and I’ll leave it at that. We’ve had a couple of — I don’t want to use the word “failed”: TV things that didn’t happen. Pilots that didn’t go, or we were actually in pre-production on a pilot when COVID hit, and then it went away. So we are back in the workshop, and we’re doing some writing right now.
	
		The desired medium for you guys is a television show.	

	Movies absolutely, and John is such a brilliant director and writer, and I’m so glad that he’s finally being seen as the filmmaker that he really is. But we’re currently investigating television as a medium that could work for us.

	
		Can you share any more?	

	I’m not trying to be overly mysterious. We’re really in the early — we do have an idea. So let’s tease the market: We have an amazing idea! We would love to make television for the people.

	“Parmesan” premieres on HBO and HBO Max on Oct. 16 at 10 p.m. PT. This interview has been edited and condensed.

schema.headline: Kate Berlant on Her HBO Special ‘Parmesan,’ the Joke That Made a Man Flip Her Off and Her Next Project With John Early

title: 7 Movies Finished by Second Directors: From ‘Batman 2’ to ‘Spartacus’
description:
Oct 16, 2026 12:49pm PT	
	

	
		7 Movies Finished by Second Directors: From ‘Batman 2’ to ‘Spartacus’
body:
Oct 16, 2026 12:49pm PT	
	

	
		7 Movies Finished by Second Directors: From ‘Batman 2’ to ‘Spartacus’
	
	
			


			
			
	

									©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection
	

		
	
				

	Hollywood is a business of people. Yesterday, the industry got a reminder of that when Warner Bros. and DC Studios announced that Steven Soderbergh will help director Matt Reeves finish production on “The Batman Part II” while Reeves deals with a family matter.

	“Just to be clear, I am not leaving ‘The Batman Part II,'” Reeves wrote on X shortly after the news broke. “I am profoundly grateful to Steven for coming to my aid during this challenging time to help me finish principal photography. Thank you to all for your concern and well wishes.” 

	This, of course, is not the first time in the history of popular cinema that an outside director stepped in to take a project over the finish line. However, few of the other switches were done with friendship, collaboration and support, as is the case with Soderbergh and Reeves. Whether it was ballooning budgets, off-camera scandal, or personal differences, Hollywood has no shortage of studios scrambling to replace their director when disaster struck.

	Here is a list of seven instances in movie history where a film had to be finished by a second director. 


			
			
	Spartacus (1960) – Anthony Mann Replaced by Stanley Kubrick
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Star Kirk Douglas, whose company, Bryna Films was producing “Spartacus,” was the one calling the shots on this classic gladiator movie, as far as the director was concerned. After two weeks of shooting, Douglas got the approval of the studio to replace Anthony Mann, an experienced director of Westerns, saying Mann had lost control and was letting co-star Peter Ustinov direct his own scenes.

	Douglas brought in Stanley Kubrick, who had directed him in “Paths of Glory,” and the film ended up winning four Oscars as well as the Golden Globe for best drama. “Spartacus” was Universal Pictures’ highest-grossing film until “Airport” 10 years later.

		
			
			
	Bohemian Rhapsody (2018) – Bryan Singer Replaced by Dexter Fletcher
			
										
					Image Credit: 20th Century Fox/Moviestore/REX/				
					
				

	“Bohemian Rhapsody” was already several months into production when director Bryan Singer failed to return to set after the Thanksgiving break. The studio temporarily halted production due to a “health matter” involving Singer — his mother was later revealed to have been ill — but reports swirled about Singer’s unreliability on set, verbal abuse and his alleged disagreements with star Rami Malek.

	Dexter Fletcher, who was previously attached to the project, was brought in to replace Singer and finish the final third of the film. Though he wasn’t mentioned in promotional materials, Singer received a sole directorial credit, in line with DGA guidelines, and Fletcher was credited as executive producer. It became the highest-grossing musical biopic until “Michael” was released, and won four Oscars in addition to a best picture nomination.

		
			
			
	Justice League (2017) – Zack Snyder Replaced by Joss Whedon
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/courtesy Everett Collection / Everett Collection				
					
				

	“Justice League” is one of the most famous recent examples of a director swap. In 2017, Zack Snyder stepped away from the film during post-production to grieve with his family after his daughter took her own life. Joss Whedon, who five years earlier hit big directing Marvel’s “Avengers,” was brought in and made sweeping changes to the film. Allegations of misconduct followed, and the understandable outrage of Snyder fans eventually led to the 2021 release of “The Snyder Cut” of “Justice League,” which clocked in at just over four hours.

	During a recent sit-down with Variety, Snyder said he’s never seen Whedon’s version of “Justice League,” given the hardships he and his family were experiencing at the time of release: “I’ve never seen it. There was a point when the movie was released that was a low point for me because the pile-on effect was so insane. Not only did I lose my daughter, but also they’ve released this version of the movie that I had nothing to do with and my name is on a movie that I didn’t make.”

		
			
			
	The Island of Dr. Moreau (1996) – Richard Stanley Replaced by John Frankenheimer
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	The production of “The Island of Dr. Moreau” was an absolutely legendary debacle. Original director Richard Stanley had been developing his pet project for four years when New Line recruited Marlon Brando to star as mad scientist Dr. Moreau. New Line wanted Roman Polanski to direct, but Brando appreciated Stanley’s vision and the film lurched into production in Australia. Bruce Willis had already dropped out of the film, with Val Kilmer stepping in and immediately acting erratically, while Brando’s daughter died by suicide before principal photography began. Two days into production, while a hurricane raged across the region, co-star Rob Morrow quit, and one day later Stanley was fired by New Line. 

	Veteran director John Frankenheimer was brought in, though the tensions continued, with both Brando and Frankenheimer tangling with Kilmer. The film’s fired production staff later reported that Stanley returned to set in a dog-man costume and acted as an extra in the film he was fired from. The film flopped and swept the Razzie Awards nominations.

		
			
			
	Superman II (1981) – Richard Donner Replaced by Richard Lester
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Father-and-son producer duo Alexander and Ilya Salkind made the bold choice in 1977 to film “Superman” and “Superman II” simultaneously, much to the chagrin of director Richard Donner. Tensions rose to such a boil that they decided to stop production on the sequel and focus on getting the first “Superman” in the can. “Superman II,” at that point, was mostly finished. After the first film dropped in 1978, Donner was pink-slipped and replaced by Richard Lester, who reshot most of “Superman II” so he could be credited as director. 

	In 1978, famed Variety columnist Army Archerd caught up with producer Pierre Spengler at a Christmas party. The French producer told Archerd that despite tensions on the first “Superman,” he was looking forward to collaborating with Donner on the sequel. Archerd then followed up with Donner, who told him of shooting the sequel with Spengler, “If he’s on it, I’m not.”

		
			
			
	Brave (2012) Brenda Chapman Replaced by Mark Andrews
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Walt Disney Co./Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				

	Brenda Chapman spent six years developing and writing the screenplay for “Brave,” which was based on her relationship with her daughter and featured Pixar’s first female protagonist. Chapman came on as Pixar’s first female director, only to be replaced by Mark Andrews due to “creative differences” with John Lasseter. 

	“I think it’s a really sad state. We’re in the 21st century and there are so few stories geared towards girls, told from a female point of view,” Chapman told the L.A. Times. “Brave” ended up winning the Oscar for best animated feature, with Chapman and Andrews credited as co-directors. 

		
			
			
	Solo: A Star Wars Story (2018) – Phil Lord and Christopher Miller Replaced by Ron Howard
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Walt Disney Co./courtesy Everett / Everett Collection				
					
				

	Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, the directors behind this year’s sci-fi box office smash “Project Hail Mary,” were originally set to direct “Solo: A Star Wars Story.” After a lengthy casting process, shooting began in January 2017, and by June 2017, Lord and Miller were out. Lucasfilm cited “creative differences” as the reason for the exit, and Ron Howard was brought in as a replacement with most of the movie already shot. It was later reported that Lucasfilm boss Kathleen Kennedy clashed with Lord and Miller over tonal issues and the loose shooting style they brought to what production considered an ironclad screenplay. 

	Hanging over all this behind-the-scenes drama was an ever-increasing production budget, which topped out at around $275 million. The movie only made $392 million worldwide, marking a major bomb for Disney and Lucasfilm. 

		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

title: Late 'Always Something There To Remind Me' Singer Peter Byrne's Royalties Income Revealed
description:
'Always Something There To Remind Me'
                          Late Singer's Family Reveals What
body:
'Always Something There To Remind Me'
                          Late Singer's Family Reveals What Peter Byrne Made Per Year In Royalties
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 16, 2026
                            2:00 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Peter Byrne, the late singer from Naked Eyes, apparently left behind a substantial estate for his three kids ...  TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs obtained by TMZ, Peter's daughter Chloe Sapienza filed to be named administrator of the rocker's estate.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sapienza says her father died without a will and had no spouse at the time of his death but notes he had 3 adult children, who would presumably inherit his assets.
      
    
            In the docs, she estimates he left behind $230K in personal and real property ... including $50K in bank accounts. She also believes he earns around $180K in annual royalties, which she says the estate would be entitled to receive to distribute to his heirs.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Peter died on September 14 following a brief illness at the age of 74. His cause of death has not been announced.
      
    
            Peter and his friend Rob Fisher are the founders of Naked Eyes.

body:
Reality TV Star Kash
                          Cops Reviewing Video That Allegedly Shows Fatal Shooting
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 16, 2026
                            12:37 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The Oakland Police Department is looking into a viral video that allegedly shows the shooting that ended reality star Kash's life.
      
    
            OPD confirmed they're looking into the clip, which is making the rounds online ... telling us it has been forwarded to the case investigator for review.
      
    
            The video is graphic ... it shows a fight breaking out between two women -- with the pair trading blows and pulling hair -- when a third woman runs up and starts smacking down at one of them.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            This third woman appears to be holding something in her hand when she runs up and starts swinging -- when suddenly the fight stops, people scamper off, and the woman on the ground lies completely still.
      
    
            We're told the OPD cannot verify the video as of yet.
      
    
            As we reported ... cops have charged Vernika Dunbar -- Kash's sister -- with involuntary manslaughter in connection with her death, claiming Vernika accidentally shot her sis when her gun went off while she was attempting to pistol-whip the other woman.
      
    
            Kash was rushed to the hospital, where she was pronounced dead.

title: Oregon School Shooting: GoFundMe Set Up For Good Samaritan Who Killed Shooter
description:
Oregon School Shooting
                          Funds Pour in For Man Who Killed Shooter
body:
Oregon School Shooting
                          Funds Pour in For Man Who Killed Shooter
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 16, 2026
                            11:37 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  October 16, 2026
                                1:19 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The Good Samaritan who put an end to a school shooter's rampage in Bend, Oregon, is getting support from people online ... who are throwing cash his way as a "thank you" for his heroic actions.
      
    
            A woman named Amy Reynolds -- a businesswoman who is based in Bend -- started a GoFundMe for Kaylub Giamanco after he rushed into Silver Rail Elementary School and neutralized a 16-year-old school shooter who had already killed 4 people
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Amy says Kaylub bravely acted out of love ... but he still has a difficult road ahead, which may require extra money.
      

            She says the GoFundMe has been set up to help Kaylub and his family afford trauma-informed therapy and mental health care, potential legal expenses connected to the shooting, lost income and everyday living expenses while Kaylub takes time off work, and any additional needs that may arise.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Amy writes, "Kaylub was there for our community in a moment of unimaginable fear. Now it's our turn to be there for him."
      
    
            The GoFundMe went live Friday morning ... and has already raised more than $2,500 out of its stated $18K goal.
      
    
            We reached out to GoFundMe ... and they told us they're monitoring the news around the shooting -- and they promise to safely hold the funds during the verification process.
      
    
            As we reported ... the school shooter used a pump-action shotgun in the attack. Cops were called around 1 PM Thursday after a caller told them the shooter had unloaded multiple shots into his car. It took officers just minutes to show up ... but Kaylub had already killed him.
